unit.can_do_en: say where I live and talk with my neighbours.

brief.situation_en: Maria speaks politely to Jukka, her upstairs neighbour.

judge.reason: Same: I live below you; only register differs (mä/minä, alapuolella/alapuolellanne).
Same greeting and question; onks/onko is register.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: There's music from your place late in the evening.

judge.reason: Same: music is heard from your place late in the evening; dropped endings only.
Same: sorry, I didn't know; only register differences.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Ei se mitään. Mä meen nukkuu kymmeneltä.
lines.text_kirja: Ei se mitään. Minä menen nukkumaan kymmeneltä.
lines.gloss_en: It's OK. I go to sleep at ten.

judge.reason: Same: it's nothing, I go to sleep at ten; meen/menen, nukkuu/nukkumaan are register.

lines.speaker: Jukka
lines.gloss_en: Of course. I'll turn the music down.

judge.reason: Same: I'll put the music on quietly; only mä/minä differs.
Same: thanks a lot; kiitti/kiitos is register.
Same: thanks for telling; et/että and sä/sinä are register.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
Asua, to live, with -n for 'I': asun.
The genitive plural of te 'you all': teidän, 'your'. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: adessive singular, with the possessive ending for your (plural)
forms.why_en: Adds -lla and -nne for 'your': alapuoli becomes alapuolellanne. Speech drops -nne: teidän alapuolella.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Means 'is...?'. The question ending -ko turns 'on' (is) into a question.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -ltä for 'from': te becomes teiltä, 'from you all'. Speech drops the last ä: teilt.
The partitive singular is used for some music: musiikki becomes musiikkia. Speech says musiikkii.
Myöhään means 'late' with a time: myöhään illalla, 'late in the evening'.
Adds -lla for a time of day: ilta becomes illalla, the t turning to l. Speech drops the last a: illal.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Means 'excuse me', a polite way to get someone's attention before asking.
Ei with -n for 'I': en, I do not.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. Speech says it the same way.
'It.' Nominative singular, referring back to the price.
The partitive singular of mikään 'any': mitään. 'Ei se mitään' means 'it's nothing, no problem'.
Mennä, to go, with -n for 'I': menen. Speech says meen.
After mennä 'to go', the verb takes -maan: nukkumaan. Speech says nukkuu.
Adds -ltä for a clock time: kymmenen becomes kymmeneltä, 'at ten'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -n for 'I': laittaa becomes laitan, tt turning to t.
As the whole thing you act on, musiikki takes -n: musiikin.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Thank you, said by the customer; in casual speech it becomes kiitti.

Speech shortens että to et. Books write että.
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.
Adds -i for the past and -t for 'you': sanoa becomes sanoit.
